name: Patellofemoral pain

diagnosisContested.note: A 2016 international consensus agrees the core criterion: pain around or behind the kneecap aggravated by at least one activity loading the joint on a flexed, weight-bearing knee. It names no definitive test; the best available is anterior knee pain during squatting (patellofemoral pain evident in 80% of those positive). The condition is still a clinical diagnosis made without a structural finding. The 2019 APTA guideline, as restated by Connell 2020 and not read directly, adds exclusion of other conditions to its diagnostic criteria (grade B), and the Dutch guideline scope also sets other knee conditions aside. Trial inclusion criteria vary considerably, and terminology is not fully settled: the consensus treats chondromalacia patella as a synonym, while the 2019 AAFP review lists it as a differential diagnosis.

avoidOrModify.movement: Squatting deep into knee flexion (beyond about 45 degrees)
avoidOrModify.rationale: In a model-based study, squats produced higher estimated patellofemoral joint stress than seated knee extension at 60, 75 and 90 degrees, and the authors suggest squatting from 45 to 0 degrees. The NATA position statement gives the same range for weight-bearing quadriceps work, at SOR C, its weakest grade. Closed-chain joint force was greatest near full flexion, and reaction force and stress were highest below parallel in barbell squats. All of this is from uninjured people or expert guidance and does not show that deeper squats cause harm. Against it, a 2026 trial used split squats from about 90 degrees to near-full extension and symptoms still improved, and Ferber's knee programme progressed to 90 degrees.

avoidOrModify.movement: Resisted seated knee extension near full straightening (about 45 to 0 degrees)
avoidOrModify.rationale: Modelled stress was higher for seated knee extension than for squats at 0, 15 and 30 degrees; an older study found the leg extension and leg press stress curves crossing at 48 degrees. The NATA statement recommends 45 to 90 degrees for non-weight-bearing work (SOR C). Clinical relevance is unproven: Cochrane found no clear short-term difference between open and closed chain work, one 49-participant study there favoured open chain long term, and a 2026 trial used knee extension from about 90 degrees to near-full extension with symptoms still improving.

avoidOrModify.movement: Activities that reproduce the knee pain, commonly squatting, stairs, running, jumping and prolonged sitting with bent knees
avoidOrModify.rationale: A clinical review advises avoiding exacerbating movements while staying as active as possible, and a guideline summary describes relative rest followed by gradual return. An uncontrolled cohort of 151 adolescents aged 10 to 14 reported high success with a 12-week programme opening with 4 weeks of activity modification using an activity ladder and pain monitoring, followed by exercise, so the activity step cannot be credited alone and may not apply to adults. Limited evidence found sitting more painful than seven other tasks. Stairs load the joint about 2.5 to 2.6 times body weight in people with the condition. One cartilage cohort is observational, in older adults, and should not be used to justify stair avoidance.

avoidOrModify.movement: High running load, such as hills or high mileage
avoidOrModify.rationale: A summary of the APTA guideline lists avoiding hills or reducing mileage for runners. Peak joint force while running was about 4.1 times body weight in this condition. In a trial of 69 runners, education on symptoms and training loads alone matched education plus exercise or gait retraining, and the authors call it a primary component. Gait retraining evidence conflicts: grade C in the APTA guideline as restated by Connell, uncertain in the 2018 consensus, and landing softer lowered knee injury risk in one prevention trial on low certainty evidence.

avoidOrModify.movement: Deep forward or side lunges, especially on a short step
avoidOrModify.rationale: Modelled loading rises with flexion. Forward lunges loaded the joint more than backward lunges in 20 uninjured women. Peak stress at 80 degrees was 3.25 MPa for side lunges against 1.91 MPa for forward lunges, and stayed under 0.85 MPa below about 30 degrees. A short step loaded more at deep angles and a long step more at shallow ones. Restricting forward travel of the front shin may lower front-leg stress while raising it in the back leg, so the usual knee-over-toe cue is not a simple fix. None of this was tested for symptoms.

At 100 degrees on the way up, modelled stress was 4.99 MPa on one leg against 2.11 MPa on two, and the authors suggest progressing two-legged to one-legged within 0 to 50 degrees before going to 100. An older study found wall squats loading more than one-leg squats at 60 to 90 degrees, so the ranking depends on the variation. The first study was in uninjured people at bodyweight; the older one used a 12-repetition maximum, so they are not directly comparable.

avoidOrModify.movement: Deep wall squats (about 90 degrees or more) with the heels close to the wall
avoidOrModify.rationale: A short heel-to-wall distance, letting the knee travel past the toes at high flexion, increased modelled loading at 90 and 100 degrees on the way up, and wall squats generally loaded more than ball squats. At 60 degrees the pattern reversed, with feet farther from the wall loading more in a weighted study, so this cue applies to deep squats only. Minimising loading may favour 0 to 50 degrees.

avoidOrModify.movement: Raising external load quickly in squats or carried-load walking
avoidOrModify.rationale: Joint force and stress rose with barbell load in experienced female lifters. In weighted-vest walking, stress rose with load and more so in women (3.8 against 2.4 MPa at 34 kg and 0 kg), and the authors suggest slower progressions for women under fixed external loads. Uninjured subjects with no clinical outcome.

avoidOrModify.movement: Exercising through more than mild knee pain
avoidOrModify.rationale: No validated threshold exists, and rules differ. NATA asks that quadriceps work be pain free. One trial accepted up to 3/10 during exercise and modified above that. A trial cited by the Dutch guideline allowed no self-reported increase in usual pain after the session or the next morning, and that guideline asks for volume and intensity to adjust continuously to pain. One crossover trial held stretches at mild discomfort but not pain. Separately, a trial with no formal pain threshold still improved, so a strict rule is not shown to be necessary.

candidateExercises.name: Side-lying hip abduction

dose.frequency: 2 days per week for 6 weeks in Kamel 2024; not specified in Raju 2024; trials in the Cochrane review averaged 3 times per week

candidateExercises.cautions: Kamel 2024 used 3 x 10 up to 3 x 20 at 2 to 3 seconds per rep with 30 seconds between sets, adding cuff or tubing resistance afterwards, which this report reads as an unloaded start. Raju 2024 used elastic resistance, lifting to about 30 degrees, for 4 weeks. Both trials are small and short.

candidateExercises.name: Banded clamshell

dose.frequency: 2 days per week for 6 weeks in Kamel 2024; twice weekly for 9 weeks in Severo-Silveira 2026

candidateExercises.cautions: Kamel 2024 names the clamshell: 3 x 10 up to 3 x 20, adding tubing resistance after that, so catalog:clamshell may suit the start. Severo-Silveira 2026 used a band clam at 1 or 3 sets of 15, then 12, then 8 reps in 3-week blocks. Raju 2024's side-lying abductor and lateral rotator work does not use the name, and matching it here is this report's reading.

candidateExercises.name: Standing banded hip abduction

dose.frequency: Prescribed at least 6 days per week for 6 weeks; about 4.8 days per week achieved

candidateExercises.cautions: Reps rose to 10 to 15 by weeks 4 to 6 for other hip exercises in the programme. Band resistance was set so the last 3 of 10 reps were challenging with good form, and an athletic trainer supervised progression. Severo-Silveira 2026 also used band hip abduction, position not stated in the data read.

candidateExercises.name: Seated banded hip external rotation

dose.frequency: Prescribed at least 6 days per week for 6 weeks; about 4.8 days per week achieved

candidateExercises.cautions: Performed seated with the knee at 90 degrees in one trial, rotating the hip to nearly 30 degrees. Progression was supervised.

candidateExercises.name: Isometric quadriceps setting

dose.frequency: Prescribed at least 6 days per week in week 1 of a 6-week programme; about 4.9 days per week achieved

candidateExercises.cautions: The trials opened did not report a hold time, so holdSeconds stays null. The trial moved to 3 sets of 15 in week 2.

candidateExercises.name: Isometric quadriceps at 60 degrees of knee flexion

dose.frequency: 5 days per week for 6 weeks

candidateExercises.cautions: The trial is weak: an implausibly large effect, inconsistent statistics and no follow-up. Performed as maximal voluntary contractions on an ISOMOVE machine, not bodyweight, with 30 seconds between sets, and 3 sets of 2 contractions is an unusually low volume. Treat as a low-confidence dose.

candidateExercises.name: Straight leg raise

dose.frequency: 2 days per week for 6 weeks in Kamel 2024; twice daily in one older trial (Colon 1988, as tabulated by Cochrane)

candidateExercises.cautions: Kamel 2024 progressed 3 x 10 to 3 x 20. Dolak, as tabulated by NATA, progressed resistance from 3% to 7% of body mass. A review of 79 studies gives 3 x 10, isometric at 0 degrees, as the median, which describes habit and not efficacy. In Raju 2024 it was part of a control programme with interferential therapy, and that group improved least.

candidateExercises.name: Terminal knee extension with band

dose.frequency: Prescribed at least 6 days per week from week 2 of a 6-week programme; about 4.9 days per week achieved

candidateExercises.cautions: NATA tabulates the same trial's standing version at 3 x 10, and Kamel 2024 used 10 degrees to full extension at 3 x 10 up to 3 x 20. It works the end-range arc where seated knee extension showed higher modelled joint stress; whether that applies to this standing exercise was not tested.

candidateExercises.name: Prone hip extension

dose.frequency: 2 days per week for 6 weeks in Kamel 2024

candidateExercises.cautions: Progressed to 3 x 20, then cuff or tubing resistance, at 2 to 3 seconds per rep with 30 seconds between sets. Named in one small trial of people with pronated feet.

candidateExercises.name: Partial-range bodyweight squat

dose.frequency: 5 days per week for 8 weeks at home in Chen 2026; prescribed at least 6 days per week for 6 weeks in Ferber 2015

candidateExercises.cautions: A depth limit must accompany the catalog exercise: to 45 degrees of knee flexion with a 2-second lowering and 2-second hold at the bottom, 2 minutes between sets, progressing every 2 weeks to at most 3 x 20 (Chen 2026, 30 adults, range not precisely monitored). Ferber 2015 used one-quarter depth with no hold in week 1, then 30-second holds in week 2. Cochrane tabulates a neutral to 30 degree semi squat held 2 seconds, 15 reps, 3 times daily.

candidateExercises.name: Wall mini-squat to 45 degrees

dose.frequency: 2 days per week for 6 weeks in Kamel 2024

candidateExercises.cautions: Progressed to 3 x 20. Median reported across trials is 3 x 10 at 0 to 45 degrees.

candidateExercises.name: Wall sit, shallow

dose.frequency: Prescribed at least 6 days per week from week 4 of a 6-week programme; about 4.9 days per week achieved

candidateExercises.cautions: The dose is for one-half depth. NATA tabulates this trial's wall slide as 3 repetitions, progressing the hold from 30 to 60 seconds and the excursion to 90 degrees. Between 60 and 90 degrees wall squats loaded the joint more than one-leg squats in modelling. A later-stage exercise under supervised progression.

candidateExercises.name: Step-down

dose.frequency: Prescribed at least 6 days per week from week 4 of a 6-week programme; about 4.9 days per week achieved

candidateExercises.cautions: The trial started on a 4-inch step, and stairs commonly aggravate this condition, so this is unsuitable as a starting exercise. A review of 79 studies gives a median of 3 sets of 20 to 10 reps on a 20 cm step, as description and not efficacy.

candidateExercises.name: Seated knee extension, limited range

dose.frequency: Median 3 sessions per week for 6 weeks across trials (Gunhamn 2025); the tabulated trial's frequency is not in the data

candidateExercises.cautions: Machine-loaded at 70% of 1RM, 90 to 45 degrees (Fukuda, as tabulated by NATA; the review median is the same range at 70% of 1RM, ranging from bodyweight to 80%). The range rests on SOR C guidance and modelling. Severo-Silveira 2026 worked from about 90 degrees to near-full extension with improvement. Cochrane reports no clear short-term pain difference between open and closed chain work.

candidateExercises.name: Leg press, limited range

dose.frequency: 3 sessions per week for 8 weeks (Peng 2015, Song 2009); the 3 x 10 tabulated trial's frequency is not in the data

candidateExercises.cautions: 3 x 10 at 70% of 1RM, 0 to 45 degrees (Fukuda, as tabulated by NATA). Peng 2015 used 5 x 10 at 60% of 1RM from 45 degrees to full extension with 2 seconds each way, a 2-second pause and 2 minutes between sets, in 17 patients. Both leg press arms in Song 2009 (89 patients) beat control. Peng found pain fell without any change in patellar tilt or offset, so alignment should not be promised as the reason. Machine-loaded.

candidateExercises.name: Split squat, loaded

dose.reps: 15 for 3 weeks, then 12 for 3 weeks, then 8 for 3 weeks
dose.frequency: Twice weekly for 9 weeks, sessions at least 48 hours apart

candidateExercises.cautions: Supervised trial in 42 women, about 4 seconds per rep, about 90 degrees to near-full extension, 1 minute between sets. Load rose if more than 2 extra reps were possible and fell if the target was missed from fatigue or knee discomfort. One set matched three sets, though a non-significant difference in a small trial does not prove equivalence. No follow-up after 9 weeks. Lunge-type depth loads the joint more in modelling, so this is not a starting exercise.

candidateExercises.name: Single-leg squat, 0 to 45 degrees

dose.frequency: Prescribed at least 6 days per week, from week 3 as single-leg quarter squats at 3 x 10 in a 6-week programme (Ferber 2015)

candidateExercises.cautions: From NATA's table of Ferber: progress to 15 reps and excursion to 90 degrees. Later stage: modelled stress on one leg was over double that on two at 100 degrees. The review median is 3 x 10, 0 to 90 degrees, from bodyweight to 70% of 1RM.

candidateExercises.name: Pillow-squeeze hip adduction

dose.frequency: 5 days per week for 6 weeks

candidateExercises.cautions: From a weak trial (see Isometric quadriceps at 60 degrees). Evidence for adding adduction conflicts: a ball squeeze during home squats lowered pain more in 30 adults (Chen 2026), and adding adduction to leg press did nothing in 89 (Song 2009). The adduction entry gives no hold, though the trial's general instruction is 5 seconds per contraction with 10 seconds rest.

candidateExercises.name: Isometric resisted hip abduction

dose.frequency: 5 days per week for 6 weeks

candidateExercises.cautions: From a weak trial (see Isometric quadriceps at 60 degrees). Done supine with knees flexed to 60 degrees against a therapist's hand, so it is untested as self-resisted work.

candidateExercises.name: Short foot exercise

dose.frequency: 2 days per week for 6 weeks

candidateExercises.cautions: Added on top of hip and knee work in 28 patients with navicular drop over 10 mm only, so it does not transfer to all feet. The source's dose description is inconsistent. Not a substitute for hip and knee exercise.

candidateExercises.name: Hamstring stretch

dose.frequency: Varied by trial, from 2 times per week to daily, in Harvie 2011

candidateExercises.cautions: Harvie 2011: 'The majority of trials examined three repetitions of 30-second duration', always bundled with strengthening. So this describes common prescription and does not show stretching works on its own. Reduced hamstring flexibility is an association that vanished against the unaffected limb. Avraham 2007, as tabulated by Cochrane, used about 3 minutes in total per session. Static stretching did not change risk in a single prevention trial. Gaitonde 2019 advises flexibility work 3 times per week for 6 to 8 weeks with no stretch dose.

candidateExercises.name: Standing quadriceps stretch

dose.frequency: Varied by trial, from 2 times per week to daily, in Harvie 2011

candidateExercises.cautions: Harvie 2011 dose, always bundled with strengthening. A 44-person trial found no difference between static and dynamic quadriceps stretching but had no no-stretch control, so it cannot show that stretching helps, and its dose was not available.

candidateExercises.name: Calf stretch

dose.frequency: Varied by trial, from 2 times per week to daily, in Harvie 2011

candidateExercises.cautions: 6 of 7 trials specifying muscles stretched the gastrocnemius. Harvie 2011 dose, always bundled with strengthening; no isolated evidence, and matching the wall version is this report's reading.

candidateExercises.name: Hip internal rotator stretch

dose.frequency: 3 sessions per week for 4 weeks

candidateExercises.cautions: Applied by a physical therapist with 20 seconds rest, held at mild discomfort but not pain. Untested as self-stretching in an app. Combined with hip strengthening, so stretching cannot be credited alone. Single-blinded crossover in which participants were not blinded, with no power analysis.

redFlags.sign: Large knee swelling, redness or increased warmth
redFlags.action: Stop exercising the knee and get prompt medical evaluation. These are not features of patellofemoral pain and can indicate infection, acute trauma or inflammatory joint disease.

redFlags.sign: Knee locking or clicking suggesting something is caught in the joint
redFlags.action: Do not attribute this to patellofemoral pain; have a clinician assess the knee. It can indicate internal derangement such as a meniscal tear or loose body.

redFlags.sign: Kneecap pain after an injury or direct trauma
redFlags.action: Have a clinician assess the knee before training it. Patellar fracture needs to be considered, using radiographs.

redFlags.sign: Kneecap dislocation, a sense of the kneecap slipping out, or apprehension when it is pushed sideways
redFlags.action: Have a clinician assess the knee. These point to patellar instability, which consensus treats as a separate subgroup and the Dutch guideline places outside its scope.

redFlags.sign: Pain and tenderness isolated to below the kneecap or the bump on the shin, especially in children and adolescents
redFlags.action: Have a clinician assess the knee. This fits tendinopathy or apophysitis more than patellofemoral pain.

redFlags.sign: Knee pain in an adolescent, particularly with a presentation that does not fit
redFlags.action: Have a clinician assess the hip as well as the knee. The APTA guideline, as restated by Connell 2020, names slipped capital femoral epiphysis as a possible cause of knee pain.

redFlags.sign: Symptoms that do not fit the expected pattern or are not resolving, or any concern about tumour or infection
redFlags.action: Refer to a clinician. The APTA guideline, as restated by Connell 2020, asks clinicians to consider red flags (tumours, infection, fracture), yellow flags and other musculoskeletal conditions in this situation.

redFlags.sign: Knee swelling or substantially increasing pain caused by the exercise
redFlags.action: Stop that exercise and get it reviewed. Cochrane defines this as an adverse event of exercise therapy. The Dutch patient survey also records increased knee pain with exercise therapy in a few people.

redFlags.sign: No improvement after a period of conservative care
redFlags.action: Return to a clinician. Timing varies: an AAFP review says imaging may help after four to eight weeks of conservative care, while the Dutch guideline reassesses at 6 weeks and reconsiders the diagnosis if there is no improvement after 12. Radiographs can help exclude osteoarthritis in people over 50.

limitations: Overall evidence stays low. Cochrane rates every main outcome very low; the Dutch guideline rates exercise evidence low in its full text and very low in a searcher's reading of its abstract; the 2021 network meta-analysis is low to very low except one moderate comparison. A 2026 systematic review (Contreras-Mora) rates strengthening evidence moderate, from its abstract only, and a core training review grades short-term function high, but these do not lift the whole body of evidence. ACCESS: the full APTA guideline (Willy 2019) was still not read: jospt.org returned HTTP 403, and its PubMed abstract contains no recommendations. All APTA grades here come through Connell 2020, a third-party appraisal narrowed to chiropractic scope, or Marra 2020; they must be checked against the original before being quoted as primary. No secondary summary could be replaced for that reason; the Dutch guideline, read in the original, was added alongside them. The 2018 consensus and Neal 2024 remain abstract only (HTTP 403). No NICE content was read (cks.nice.org.uk returned 403; NICE search reported 4 unread results), and the AAOS guideline index was not checked, so absence of those guidelines is not established. Cochrane was reached through PMC; one searcher read the first 200,000 of 502,300 characters, an earlier pass reported all but 2,300 characters, and another searcher got only the abstract and summary through a failed route. Several other full texts were read by targeted passage or missed final sections. Supplements or linked protocols holding exercise details for Xiong 2025, Xiao 2026 and Vasconcelos 2024 were not read. Marra 2020, Gaitonde 2019, Ferber 2015 and Raju 2024 were reopened by the independent check. CONTRADICTIONS. Hip plus knee: favoured by Cochrane, the 2016 and 2018 consensus statements, Nascimento 2018, Halabi 2025 and Neal 2022 (SMD 1.02 for pain), but Hansen 2023 found quadriceps and hip programmes equivalent, Hott 2019 and 2020 found neither beat free activity plus education, Winters 2021 found no winner, and Neal 2024 frames care as knee with or without hip. Khayambashi 2014 favoured hip over quadriceps, against Hansen 2023. Sequencing: NATA recommends 3 weeks of isolated gluteal work first (SOR B), while trials of targeted programmes show no clear overall advantage. Mechanism: Nascimento 2018 and Holden 2021 found benefit without strength change or mediation, whereas Nunes 2026 found strong correlations between strength and pain change (r -0.75 and -0.91), and it cannot show cause. Hip weakness: not a risk factor (Neal 2019; NATA), and higher hip abduction strength was a risk factor in adolescents, although hip strengthening helps. Education: Winters 2021 and Esculier 2018 show education close to exercise at some time points, whereas Pazzinatto 2026 found education worse than exercise overall, though not when delivered by a health professional. Its pain CI is printed in PubMed as 1.46 (0.6 to 2.56), which is asymmetric. Volume: de Oliveira 2023's exploratory meta-regression favours 17 to 27 sets per session for function only, whereas Severo-Silveira 2026 found 1 set matched 3 and Young 2018 found no dosing trend. Marra 2020's statement that higher volumes work best is likewise unsupported by the latter two. Passive care: the APTA guideline as restated gives dry needling and isolated manual therapy grade A against, while the 2018 consensus calls dry needling uncertain, Neal 2022 reports SMD 2.30 for lower-quadrant manual therapy on function, and Neal 2024 lists manual therapy as a support. Orthoses: APTA grade A short term, consensus supported, but the Dutch guideline allows them only after 6 weeks without clinically relevant change, and a Cochrane orthoses review found no added benefit over physiotherapy. Braces: APTA grade B against and null as a treatment adjunct, yet braces lowered onset in a prevention review (RR 0.40). Taping: APTA grade B tailored use and Wallis 2021 consistent, against Souto 2024 and Callaghan 2012 null. Visual feedback: NATA SOR A for movement retraining against APTA grade B against visual biofeedback during exercise. Depth: modelled limits and SOR C guidance suggest 0 to 45 degrees weight bearing and 90 to 45 non-weight bearing, while trials using about 90 degrees to near-full extension improved. Hip adduction: Chen 2026 positive against Song 2009 null. Saltychev 2018 is dissenting: over 80% of 37 trials showed no clinically significant benefit. Cochrane's hip plus knee estimate is -2.20 in its abstract and -2.02 in its summary table, with the same CI, which fits -2.20. Registration: Xiong 2025 and Xiao 2026 give the same trial number, ChiCTR2400087664, for trials that appear different, which is unresolved. PROCESS: Blazey 2024 found only 2 of 22 consensus panels included a patient and 7 of 22 reported an established method. CPG adherence has no randomised outcomes yet: Farrokhi 2025 is a retrospective pilot with missing data and a guideline author, and knEE-CAPP is a protocol. DOSES are what individual trials used, usually supervised; none is a validated optimum. Holden 2018 found no trial reported a complete prescription, and Gunhamn 2025's medians describe habit rather than efficacy. The Hasan 2025 doses should be treated with caution. Null sets means the source gave no usable per-exercise value, and the isometric quadriceps setting hold remains unreported. No evidence-based pain threshold exists: the figures here are trial rules. Harm data are thin: Winters 2021 dropped adverse events for lack of data, and few trials recorded them actively. Biomechanical limits come largely from uninjured people and estimate stress, not outcomes. Stretching evidence is indirect or bundled. Most stretch and hip data are short term, and Neal 2022 found no intervention adequately tested beyond 3 months. Rathleff 2019 was uncontrolled and covers ages 10 to 14 only. Blood flow restriction, covered by Hou 2026 and trials, needs a cuff and is not an unsupervised app option. Red flags come from clinical reviews and guideline restatements and are not validated screening rules. An independent check then opened every source; see verification for its limits. This is general information and not diagnosis or treatment.

valuesCorrected: gunhamn2025 knee extension median intensity: 70 to 80% of 1RM changed to 70% of 1RM, range bodyweight to 80%.
ophey2025 additional treatments: after 6 to 12 weeks changed to after 6 weeks, as the guideline states for patellofemoral pain.
ophey2025 survey: 52 respondents split into 43 patellofemoral pain and 9 patellar tendinopathy; the 12 (40%) dissatisfied are patellofemoral pain patients.
holden2021 -0.13 (-0.49 to 0.23) relabelled: it is abduction strength on pain-free squats, not pain.
deoliveira2023 17 to 27 sets relabelled as function only; the paper found no volume association with pain.
ishida2025 9% relabelled as peak stress; the at-90-degrees figure in the paper is reaction force, 11%.
gaitonde2019 four to eight weeks relabelled: it is when imaging may help, not a return-to-clinician rule.
Stretch frequency (3 exercises): "not stated separately" changed to 2 times per week to daily, from harvie2011 Table 2; hamstring entry adds gaitonde2019 flexibility schedule.
ferber2015 single-leg squat start week: not confirmed changed to week 3. Partial squat: 30-second holds in week 2 added to "no hold".

hasan2025 quadriceps isometric: machine-based maximal contractions, bodyweightOrHold changed to false. Hip abduction: supine at 60 degrees against a therapist, bodyweightOrHold changed to false. Pillow squeeze: general 5-second instruction noted.
Deep wall squats: escamilla2023 loading limited to 90 and 100 degrees on ascent, with the reversal at 60 degrees from escamilla2009 added.
One-legged squats: "bodyweight only" limited to escamilla2025, since escamilla2009 used a 12-repetition maximum.
rathleff2019: 4 weeks of activity modification restated as the opening of a 12-week programme.
jellad2021: "unblinded" changed to single-blinded with participants not blinded.
accessLevel of marra2020, gaitonde2019, ferber2015 and raju2024: not_reconfirmed changed to full_text, all reopened.
connell2020 markdown link changed from PubMed to the PMC url in the JSON.
unverifiable: Sources marked abstract_only, including collins2018, neal2024 and willy2019, were checked against the abstract only. Willy 2019 holds no recommendations in its abstract, so every APTA grade rests on connell2020 or marra2020.
Full texts were searched for the claims made and not read end to end. cochrane2015 was queried across characters 0 to 500,000 of 502,300.
contrerasmora2026, wang2024 and hou2026 have PMC copies but stay abstract_only because their claims were checked only against the abstract.
Publisher pages at BMJ and JOSPT were not opened. Their DOIs redirect and match the PubMed records, but that does not confirm the landing page.
ferber2015 prints step height as 4-inch (3.6 cm), which is internally inconsistent, so the true height is uncertain.
hasan2025 being implausibly large is this report's judgement (AKPS +38 in 6 weeks, in Table 4), not a statement by the paper.
ophey2025 abstract gives very low and low GRADE for the two conditions without clearly mapping them; its text gives low for exercise in patellofemoral pain.
